Unrighteousness
ŭn-rī´teous-ness
n. (violation of what is right; rendering Hebrew avel, evel, Greek adikia)
From un-, not, and righteousness, Anglo-Saxon rihtwisnes, right-wiseness. The word is not a mood but a measurement: what fails to conform to the rule.

Biblical Definition

Unrighteousness is conformity failed — whatever departs from the standard of God's own character. Scripture first defines it by its absence in Him: “he is my rock, and there is no unrighteousness in him” (Psa 92:15). The law then applies it in the two places men most easily excuse themselves: the courtroom and the marketplace. “Ye shall do no unrighteousness in judgment: thou shalt not respect the person of the poor, nor honour the person of the mighty” (Lev 19:15), and “Ye shall do no unrighteousness in judgment, in meteyard, in weight, or in measure” (Lev 19:35). Partial verdicts and short weights are the same sin. Paul then makes unrighteousness the ground of universal wrath and adds the phrase that exposes the mechanism: men “hold the truth in unrighteousness” (Rom 1:18) — they do not merely lack the truth; they hold it down, suppress it, because it condemns what they intend to keep doing.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines unrighteousness as injustice, a violation of the divine law or of the plain principles of justice and equity, and as wickedness, or any deviation from rectitude.

UNRIGHT´EOUSNESS, n. Injustice; a violation of the divine law, or of the plain principles of justice and equity.

2. Wickedness; any deviation from rectitude.

3. In Scripture, it often denotes the whole state of a man out of Christ, as opposed to the righteousness of faith.

All unrighteousness is sin. 1 John v.

Key Scripture

Rom 1:18 — "For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men, who hold the truth in unrighteousness;"

Lev 19:15 — "Ye shall do no unrighteousness in judgment: thou shalt not respect the person of the poor, nor honour the person of the mighty: but in righteousness shalt thou judge thy neighbour."

Psa 92:15 — "To shew that the LORD is upright: he is my rock, and there is no unrighteousness in him."

Lev 19:35 — "Ye shall do no unrighteousness in judgment, in meteyard, in weight, or in measure."

Modern Corruption

Unrighteousness reduced to structural disparity on one side and to private impropriety on the other — while Romans 1:18 names the real mechanism, the deliberate suppression of a truth already known.

expand to see more

Romans 1:18 is the verse the age cannot afford to read. Paul does not describe men who never heard; he describes men who hold the truth in unrighteousness, pressing down a knowledge they possess because it stands in the way of what they mean to do. That makes unbelief a moral act before it is an intellectual one, and it explains why arguments so rarely settle these matters. The problem was never the evidence.

Leviticus 19:15 then cuts across every partisan account of injustice. It forbids partiality toward the mighty, which is expected — and partiality toward the poor in the same breath, which is not. A framework that assigns guilt and innocence by group standing violates the verse from whichever direction it approaches. And verse 35 keeps the whole matter from floating into abstraction by naming meteyard, weight, and measure: unrighteousness is finally something a man does with a scale, a verdict, or a wage.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew avel (H5766), injustice, wrong; Greek adikia (G93), the alpha-privative of dike — what is not according to right; the word Paul pairs with ungodliness in Rom 1:18.

expand to see more

Hebrew avel (H5766) — injustice, unrighteousness, wrong; the standing prohibition of Lev 19:15 and 19:35.

Greek adikia (G93) — unrighteousness, iniquity; all unrighteousness is sin (1Jn 5:17), and the truth is held down in it (Rom 1:18).

Greek katecho (G2722) — to hold down, suppress, restrain; Paul's verb for what men do to the truth they already have.

Usage

"“There is no unrighteousness in him” — the standard is a Person, not a code."

"“Thou shalt not respect the person of the poor, nor honour the person of the mighty” — partiality forbidden both ways."

"“Who hold the truth in unrighteousness” — unbelief as a moral act."
